historical_timeline.summary: Born in San Francisco as John Griffith Chaney; raised by his mother and his stepfather, John London.
Works from boyhood as an oyster pirate, fish patrolman, seaman and tramp.
Klondike gold rush; comes home with scurvy.
Marries; two daughters are born in 1901 and 1902; divorced in 1905, he marries again in November 1905.
The Call of the Wild brings international fame; writes 1,000 words a day for the rest of his life.
Buys the first land of his ranch at Glen Ellen.
Sails on the Snark; sores, swollen peeling hands and a silvery skin in the South Pacific; gives up the voyage in Australia.
Wolf House burns; John Barleycorn is published the same year.
War correspondent at Vera Cruz; ill with dysentery and rheumatism.
Returns from five months in Hawaii; sails there again on December 16, 1915.
Dies at his ranch at 40 of uraemia following renal colic; he had refused his doctors' advice to stop drinking and change his habits. A later story of a morphine overdose or suicide is disputed.

claims.statement: He was born on January 12, 1876, in San Francisco, and his birth certificate named him John Griffith Chaney. His mother, Flora Wellman, had lived with William Chaney, an astrologer, who left before the birth; she married John London, who adopted and raised the boy.

claims.statement: On the voyage of his yacht Snark through the South Pacific (1907 to 1909), in the Solomon Islands he had sores that a physician in Fiji called yaws and a missionary said were not; his hands swelled and peeled and his toenails thickened, a malady the Australian specialists could not name; he spent five weeks in hospital in Australia, gave up the voyage, and blamed tropical light. He also had a 'silvery skin' that doctors called by old names for leprosy, which cleared without treatment in California.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own published account, recorded as he gave it; the modern diagnosis of these conditions is not settled (CLM-0007).

claims.statement: Physicians writing since have interpreted his illnesses differently: the 'silvery skin' has been read as psoriasis; one review proposed that mercury used to treat yaws damaged his kidneys and caused a dermatitis of the hands, feet and face; others suggested lupus, gout, and the effects of tobacco, alcohol and diet on his blood pressure and kidneys. None is established.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective and disputed; none is used as a diagnosis for him. The modern episode's kidney disease has its own synthetic cause.

claims.statement: In John Barleycorn (1913) he wrote of his drinking from the first time he got drunk, at five years old. He held that he was no born alcoholic and had acquired the taste, and described how at the ranch, after writing his thousand words between nine and eleven each morning, he began to take a cocktail before midday dinner and then alone, 'not for the sake of the taste, but for the effect of the drink.'
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of heavy drinking, recorded in his words; it anchors the modern alcohol use disorder but does not make a diagnosis for him.

claims.statement: Whether morphine contributed to his death is disputed. A story that he took his own life began after his death and was spread by a 1938 biographical novel that described empty morphine vials; his attending physicians denied it, and historians, a pharmacist and physicians have argued against it, noting that he had taken morphine for pain for some time and that failing kidneys would have let a usual dose build up.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Disputed; the record takes neither side, and nothing about suicide or overdose is used in the modern episode. Recorded only as later history.

source_links.locator: The rumor was apparently started shortly after London's death; Doctors Deny Jack London Killed Self; Stone ... two empty vials labeled morphine sulfate and atropine sulfate; with London's use of morphine for possibly as long as three years, he would have developed a tolerance; a dose that normally might have been therapeutic might easily have been rendered toxic by his weakened renal condition

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Alcohol use disorder with chronic kidney disease and hypertension in a working writer: a 39-year-old novelist who writes a thousand words every morning on his ranch comes in tired, with swollen ankles, and is found to have a blood pressure of 158/98, an eGFR of 43 and albumin in the urine, and to drink heavily. The episode covers the AUDIT, the DSM-5-TR criteria and PEth; liver tests, FIB-4 and elastography; outpatient withdrawal management with a withdrawal-risk score and thiamine; medicine for alcohol use disorder chosen with kidney function in mind (naltrexone, with acamprosate needing a lower dose at his creatinine clearance and avoided below 30 mL/min); CKD staging by KDIGO 2024 with eGFR and urine albumin, the cause (hypertension and two years of daily naproxen, without stones or gout), ultrasound, the kidney failure risk equation and mineral tests; blood pressure under KDIGO 2021 and the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline with an angiotensin receptor blocker at the maximum dose and potassium and creatinine checks; an SGLT2 inhibitor once he is abstinent, because heavy drinking raises the risk of ketoacidosis; analgesic and opioid safety, with no NSAIDs, a lower acetaminophen limit and naltrexone's opioid blockade; the safety assessment and lethal-means counseling; tobacco; vaccinations in kidney and liver disease; and a plan that protects his morning writing hours.

hpi.narrative: Mr. London stopped drinking on the morning after his intake visit and took the five-day chlordiazepoxide taper as prescribed, with a daily telephone check from the nurse. The first three days brought sweats, a tremor and poor sleep, at worst a CIWA-Ar of 11 on the second day, with no hallucinations or seizures; by the fifth day the tremor had gone, and he has had no alcohol since. He missed two mornings of writing and has written his thousand words every other day. He has taken losartan 50 mg daily without dizziness and stopped naproxen; acetaminophen eases his knee. His ankles are less swollen. He has seen the clinic's addiction counselor once. The insurance examination report has arrived, confirming a creatinine of 1.7 mg/dL about fourteen months ago. Ultrasound and liver elastography were done this morning. He sees Dr. Mbatha-Rasmussen of nephrology this afternoon.

assessment.assessment: Chronic kidney disease, stage G3b A2 by KDIGO 2024: an eGFR of 42 to 43 with albumin 240 mg/g, and a creatinine already 1.7 mg/dL fourteen months ago, so it has lasted more than three months; high risk on the KDIGO heat map. Normal-sized echogenic kidneys, a bland sediment without blood, moderate rather than heavy albuminuria and long-standing untreated hypertension point to hypertensive kidney disease, with two years of daily naproxen adding harm. There are no stones or obstruction, and no gout attacks; the uric acid of 8.4 mg/dL does not need treatment without gout. Alcohol raises blood pressure but is not itself a usual cause of this picture. Nothing suggests a glomerulonephritis or another disease that needs a biopsy now; hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology are drawn today, and a biopsy would be reconsidered for blood in the urine, rising albumin or a fall in eGFR without explanation. A cystatin C estimate is not needed now, since no decision hinges on it. 25-hydroxyvitamin D was not drawn and should be

Aim for a systolic below 120 by standardized office measurement if he tolerates it, as KDIGO 2021 advises, and at least below 130/80 as the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline does. Losartan should go to the maximum tolerated dose, 100 mg, because it lowers albuminuria as well as pressure; potassium 4.9 and a 3 percent rise in creatinine are acceptable. Check potassium and creatinine two to four weeks after each change; accept a creatinine rise of up to 30 percent. Less than 2 g of sodium a day; amlodipine would be the next step

He meets the KDIGO 2024 recommendation for an SGLT2 inhibitor (eGFR 20 or more with albumin 200 mg/g or more), which slows kidney decline whether or not there is diabetes. But heavy drinking, missed meals and vomiting raise the risk of ketoacidosis on these drugs, even without diabetes. I advise waiting until he has been abstinent for some weeks and is eating regularly, then dapagliflozin 10 mg daily with written sick-day rules, and potassium and creatinine two to four weeks after starting, expecting an early dip in eGFR

Naltrexone is the better choice. It is cleared mainly by the liver, needs no dose change at his kidney function, and his liver tests are falling and under three times normal; he takes no opioids. Acamprosate is cleared by the kidneys: at a creatinine clearance of 30 to 50 mL/min the dose must be cut to 333 mg three times a day and below 30 it should not be used, and with his clearance near 58 and likely to change, and a three-times-a-day schedule he says he would not keep, it is a second choice. The outpatient chlordiazepoxide taper was reasonable for his kidneys, since it is cleared by the liver, and safe for a liver without cirrhosis; in a man with cirrhosis or worse liver function a shorter-acting benzodiazepine would be preferred. Disulfiram is not advised

No naproxen, ibuprofen, high-dose aspirin or other oral anti-inflammatory medicines, which cut kidney blood flow and caused part of this damage. Acetaminophen is the first choice, kept to 2,000 mg a day after heavy drinking. A short course of a topical anti-inflammatory gel on a small area is acceptable, because blood levels are low. No opioids or tramadol: naltrexone blocks opioids, morphine's active products build up when the kidneys are weak, and opioids add risk in early recovery. Any new medicine should be checked for kidney dosing, and iodinated contrast used only with precautions
